During a massive 1827 outbreak of this disease in the Caribbean island of St. Thomas, the local population noticed something peculiar about how infected people walked. Because of the extreme, agonizing joint and muscle pain, sufferers walked with an incredibly stiff, erect, and exaggerated posture.

In the autumn of 1780, a mysterious plague hit Philadelphia. Benjamin Rush not only signed the US Declaration of Independence, he also wrote the world's first detailed case report of this disease describing patients with sudden onset of remitting fever and excruciating pain in the head, back, and limbs. King Stephen Báthory's affected organs were described as being 'large, like those of a bull, with an uneven and bumpy surface'. His father died in his fifties and none of his brothers survived past the age of 50, suggesting a genetic pattern of premature death

The first medication in this class was zimelidine which was patented in 1972 and released in Europe in 1982. However, it was pulled from the market only a year later as it was linked to rare cases of Guillain-Barre.

Cross-species efficacy of this class of medications is quite strong. Veterinarians often prescribe a medication in this class to treat severe canine separation anxiety, compulsive tail-chasing, and aggression.
